$comment: Inputs for the fnmatch/shlex differential oracle (DECISIONS.md D-0200, docs/differential-oracle.md). Committed rather than generated so both halves build the identical vector, and small enough to read. The fnmatch corpus is the cartesian product patterns x names, in that order (pattern outer, name inner); the shlex corpora are flat lists. Regenerate the vector with scripts/oracle/dump_fnmatch_shlex.py -- never by hand.

fnmatch.$comment_patterns: Every spec the shipped roles.json actually renders, plus the bracket-expression and star-compression territory that a hand-rolled glob gets wrong. The empty-range, negated-empty-range and set-operation cases are the branches CPython grew deliberately and a rewrite never has.
fnmatch.$comment_names: Subjects, including the ones that separate fnmatch's `*` (which crosses `/`) from shell globbing's (which does not) -- the difference that would silently narrow a fence.
fnmatch.$comment_astral: The tail of both lists is astral (non-BMP) territory, added after a review found that compiling the translated regex WITHOUT the u flag made every atom match one UTF-16 code unit while CPython's fnmatch matches one code point -- so `?` did not match an emoji and a rule using it denied less than interlock denies. The 4,425 comparisons before this addition all missed it, because not one input contained a character outside the BMP. That gap was part of the defect, so it is closed here: a bare astral character, one inside a bracket expression, astral range endpoints in both directions (including the inverted range that exercises CPython's empty-range removal), an astral character adjacent to a BMP one, and BMP non-ASCII for the boundary.
fnmatch.$comment_boundary: U+FFFF is the last BMP code point and U+10000 the first astral one. Both sides of that boundary are present deliberately: the code-point helpers in src/fencing/fnmatch.ts compare and slice by code point, and an off-by-one there (> 0xffff where >= 0xffff was meant, or a surrogate-pair split) shows up on exactly these inputs and on no others. The corpus carried the astral side alone until a verifier pointed out that a boundary tested from one side is not tested.

$comment_shlex_split: Command lines the renderer actually parses, plus the backslash and quoting territory. Entries that CPython rejects (unterminated quote, trailing escape) are included deliberately: the vector records the raised error, because 'both sides refuse' is as much a parity claim as 'both sides agree on the tokens'.
shlex_split: /usr/bin/python3 '/a dir with spaces/hook.py' --role worker --fence '/a dir with spaces/state/fence.json'
$comment_shlex_quote: Strings the renderer quotes into a hook command line. The unsafe-character boundary is exact in CPython (`@%+=:,./-` and word characters are safe; everything else is not), and an approximation of it either over-quotes -- changing bytes the restart diff compares -- or under-quotes, which is the hole.
$comment_pypath: Inputs for the posixpath.normpath / os.path.expanduser transcription (src/fencing/pypath.ts). normpath decides whether a sandbox deny rule covers a candidate path, and Node's path.posix.normalize is NOT the same function -- it keeps a trailing slash and collapses a leading '//'. expanduser is generated with HOME pinned to ORACLE_HOME below, because an environment-dependent oracle compares two environments rather than two implementations.

pypath.$comment_expanduser_deviation: CPython resolves ~someuser through the pwd database. Node has no equivalent, so src/fencing/pypath.ts returns those paths unchanged -- which is the branch CPython itself takes when the lookup fails. expanduser stays a faithful transcription, so the deviation is still real here and the inputs below are kept in the corpus rather than deleted from it: a deviation removed from the oracle is a deviation nobody can see. The test asserts continuo returns them unchanged AND that CPython did something different, so the day the two agree by accident this entry goes stale loudly. What changed is the blast radius: the deviation is now CONTAINED rather than merely accepted, because parseSandboxEntry in src/fencing/rules.ts REFUSES a ~user path on posix with RuleSyntaxError, so no fence rule can be built on an unresolved ~user path. See DECISIONS.md D-0203.
pypath.$comment_normalize_path: rules._normalize_path, the COMPOSED function -- posixpath.normpath(os.path.expanduser(p).replace(os.sep, "/")) -- as distinct from the two halves already pinned above. os.sep is platform-dependent in the source and stays that way in the port, so the vector records BOTH compositions: the posix one (posixpath.expanduser, os.sep '/') and the Windows one (ntpath.expanduser, os.sep '\\'), and the test compares against the one for the platform it is running on. That is not a convenience: on Windows a sandbox deny entry "~\\.aws" is ONE component to ntpath -- the backslash terminates the user field -- so interlock expands it and denies the read, while a posix-only transcription would return it unchanged and not deny. HOME, USERPROFILE and USERNAME are pinned on both sides for the duration of the call, because an environment-dependent oracle compares two environments rather than two implementations.
pypath.$comment_normalize_path_accepted_deviati: The ~user deviation of the expanduser section, reaching the composed function. Two things are true of these inputs and both are why they are listed rather than compared: continuo returns them UNCHANGED (CPython's own lookup-failed branch, see expanduser_accepted_deviations and DECISIONS.md D-0203), and the value CPython produced is the GENERATING MACHINE's pwd entry -- posixpath.expanduser reads the password database, so "/root" in the vector is a fact about the machine that ran the dump and not about CPython. Comparing it would make the oracle depend on the runner. Asserted in both directions all the same: continuo must pass them through, and CPython must have done something else.

$comment_pystr: Inputs for the Python string-semantics helpers in src/fencing/rules.ts. repr() shapes refusal MESSAGE text, and the ported tests assert both halves of a refusal (type and message) through expectRefusal -- so a repr that double-quotes where CPython single-quotes turns a faithful translation into a failing one, or, worse, makes a sloppy assertion pass for the wrong reason. strip() differs from JavaScript's trim() on U+FEFF alone, which is exactly the kind of difference nobody discovers by reading. repr_nonstring names values rather than embedding them, because JSON cannot express the distinction between Python's int and float.
$comment_pyregex: Inputs for the CPython-regex-dialect translator (src/fencing/pyregex.ts). renderer.py:_check_forbidden_allow compiles AUTHOR-SUPPLIED patterns out of the global config and runs pattern.search() over every permissions.allow entry, so CPython's regex dialect is part of the fence exactly as fnmatch's glob dialect is -- and the translator is ~1,000 lines of transcription, which is the artefact class this oracle exists for. The corpus is the cartesian product patterns x subjects (pattern outer, subject inner). For each pattern the vector records either re.search's answer on every subject or the re.error message re.compile raised, because 'both sides refuse this pattern' is as much a parity claim as 'both sides agree on the match'.

pyregex.$comment_patterns: Everything the module claims to handle -- $ before a trailing newline, . versus \r and U+2028/U+2029, the Unicode \w \d \s \b, {,n}, (?P<n>)/(?P=n), inline (?i)(?s)(?m), \A \Z, character classes -- plus the three patterns the shipped src/fencing/roles.json actually compiles, plus the constructs the translator deliberately REFUSES. The refusals are in the corpus rather than left out of it: a fail-closed translator's refusal set IS part of its behaviour, and an unlisted refusal is one nobody can see go stale.
pyregex.$comment_subjects: Allow entries a role document can carry, crossed with the alphabet that separates the two dialects: a trailing newline (Python's $ matches before it, JavaScript's does not), a bare \r and U+2028/U+2029 (JavaScript's . excludes them, Python's does not), the whitespace characters str.isspace() and JavaScript's \s disagree about in both directions, Unicode word and digit characters, the Turkish dotted and dotless I (where the two case foldings part company), and astral characters with the last BMP code point beside them.
pyregex.$comment_refused: Patterns CPython ACCEPTS and src/fencing/pyregex.ts refuses -- divergence class 1 in that module's header. The translator is fail-closed by construction: anything not on its equivalence list throws rather than being copied through on the assumption that it means the same thing in both dialects (the assumption that made `.` a silent hole). Interlock renders these documents and continuo refuses them, which stops a spawn rather than admitting one and says so out loud. The test asserts BOTH halves -- continuo refuses AND CPython compiled -- so an entry that goes stale fails instead of quietly licensing nothing. The lookbehind entries are the over-refusal side of the fixed-width rule: CPython computes a min and a max width for the body and accepts it when they agree, so `(?<=ab|cd)e`, `(?<=a|b)c`, `(?<=a{1,1})b`, `(?<=a{2}?)b`, a backreference to a fixed-width group and a named group referenced back inside the same lookbehind are all legal there. Reproducing that analysis is not worth its own bug surface, so the walk refuses every construct that CAN vary a body's width -- alternation, `* + ?`, a range repeat, any backreference -- and the fixed-width forms it still accepts (`(?<=ab)c`, `(?<!ab)c`, `(?<=a{2})b`) are in `patterns` above with subjects that exercise them.
pyregex.$comment_refusal_message_deviations: Patterns BOTH sides refuse, with different wording -- divergence class 4. Two causes, kept in one list because the assertion is the same: a pattern the walk rejects before CPython's own parser would have reached the same fault (it recognises `(?(` as an unsupported group where CPython gets as far as resolving the group reference), and a pattern that survives the walk and is rejected by `new RegExp`, whose SyntaxError wording is the engine's. Everywhere else the message this module authors carries CPython's exact wording INCLUDING the `at position N` suffix, and the test compares it byte for byte -- the offset is what tells an operator which `[` in a long pattern was never closed. Asserted in both directions: both sides must still refuse, and the messages must still differ.
pyregex.$comment_python_only_refusals: CLOSED, and kept as an empty list so the mechanism stays wired. It held `(?<=a+)b` and `(?<!a+)b`: CPython rejects them (`look-behind requires fixed-width pattern`) and this translator compiled them, because JavaScript's lookbehind is variable-width and the walk had nothing to say about it -- the 'interlock refuses, continuo renders' direction the module header names as the dangerous one. This corpus is what found it. src/fencing/pyregex.ts now refuses a lookbehind body it cannot prove fixed-width, so those two patterns moved into the ordinary refusal comparison above, where the message is checked against CPython's byte for byte; the lookbehinds CPython accepts and the new rule over-refuses moved into `refused`. An entry added here again would be a NEW instance of the same class, not this one.
pyregex.$comment_ignorecase_match_deviations: [pattern, subject] pairs where both sides compile and the MATCH differs because of case folding -- divergence class 3. `(?i)` becomes RegExp's `i` under `u`, which is Unicode SIMPLE case folding; CPython's IGNORECASE is full folding over the same tables, so it folds the Turkish dotted and dotless I onto ASCII `i` and JavaScript does not. CPython therefore matches MORE, which for a forbidden_allow_regex means interlock forbids an allow entry that continuo lets through: the fail-OPEN direction, and the reason these pairs are in the corpus rather than left out of it. Asserted in both directions.
pyregex.$comment_astral_anchor_match_deviations: [pattern, subject] pairs where both sides compile and the match differs at an ASTRAL character -- found by this corpus, on its first run, and previously unrecorded anywhere. `$`, `\Z` and `(?m)^`/`(?m)$` are compiled away into explicit lookarounds (`(?![\s\S])`, `(?<![\s\S])`) because JavaScript's notion of a line terminator is four characters wide and Python's is one. Under the `u` flag those lookarounds are satisfied at an index BETWEEN the two surrogate halves of an astral character -- neither half can be matched as a whole code point from that position, so the index looks like both start-of-string and end-of-string -- and the engine does attempt a match there. So `\A\Z` and `(?m)^$` match a string made of one emoji, which CPython does not, and `\Z` reports the wrong offset in a string that ends after one. The direction is over-matching, which for a forbidden_allow_regex means continuo forbids an allow entry interlock permits: fail-closed and loud, not a hole -- which is why it is recorded here instead of blocking the belt. Closing it means the emulations anchoring themselves to a code-point boundary, which is a change to src/fencing/pyregex.ts and not to this corpus. Asserted in both directions.

$comment_pyjson: Inputs for the json.dumps / json.loads transcription (src/fencing/pyjson.ts). Interlock writes every durable fencing artefact through json.dumps and the restart path compares those artefacts BY BYTES, so a serialiser that agrees with CPython on every value except one produces a permanent 'the fence changed' rather than a slightly different file. The values are given as JSON SOURCE TEXTS and parsed by each side's loader, which is the only way to express a mapping whose keys are integer-like and out of order: a JavaScript object literal hoists '10' in front of '2' and no amount of care while building one avoids it.

pyjson.$comment_dumps: Crossed with dumps_options (text outer, option inner). Covers sort_keys both ways, indent including CPython's distinction between indent=0 and indent=None, explicit separators, nesting, non-ASCII under ensure_ascii both ways, astral characters (which json.dumps spells as a SURROGATE PAIR of four-digit escapes, not \U), U+007F (which CPython escapes under ensure_ascii and leaves raw without it), and integer-like keys out of order.
pyjson.$comment_dumps_options: Named rather than embedded because the two sides spell the keyword arguments differently (sort_keys / sortKeys). The dump script and the test each hold the same table; the names here are what pairs them.
pyjson.$comment_dumps_numbers: Number formatting is float.__repr__, not String(n): CPython switches to exponential once the decimal point sits past digit 16 and writes a two-digit exponent, JavaScript waits until 1e21 and writes one. Named rather than embedded for the reason pystr.repr_nonstring is: JSON cannot express the int/float distinction, and this section is precisely about it.
pyjson.$comment_dumps_number_accepted_deviation: The residue that survives the number round-trip repair, pinned here rather than left as prose. Every value in dumps_numbers is built IN CODE on both sides -- a Python literal in the dump script, a TypeScript literal in the test -- so there is no document and no recorded spelling: an integral float written as a JavaScript literal is the same double as the int, and this port prints the int spelling where CPython prints 1.0 / 1000000000000000.0. A document that spells the same numbers round-trips exactly; see number_documents, which is where the repair is measured. Asserted in BOTH directions -- the port must produce the int spelling AND CPython must have produced something else -- so the entry fails loudly if it ever goes stale.
pyjson.$comment_loads: pyJsonLoads exists for ONE property that JSON.parse cannot give: the source key order. A dict preserves insertion order for every key; a JavaScript object hoists integer-like keys to the front in ascending numeric order, so {"10": .., "2": ..} comes back in the wrong order and takes repr(), _check_placeholders and the order of the refusal reasons with it. Every text below is valid JSON: the wording of a PARSE ERROR is JavaScript's, deliberately (docs/differential-oracle.md section 7, exception classification), and is not claimed here.
pyjson.$comment_number_documents: The number round trip: loads -> dumps, plus type(x).__name__ for every number, over the two things JavaScript's single number type loses. (1) int/float provenance: CPython parses 1 and 1.0 to different types, so json.dumps re-emits them differently and type(x).__name__ answers differently -- visible in the fence ledger, where interlock writes \"at\": 0.0 and this port wrote \"at\": 0, and in a refusal that said got int where interlock says got float. (2) exact integers past 2**53: JSON.parse(\"9007199254740993\") is 9007199254740992 and the authored value is gone before anything can serialise it. Every document here has an OBJECT or ARRAY root, which is not incidental: a spelling is recorded on the container slot, because a JavaScript number is a primitive that cannot carry one without breaking === on every ordinary number in the tree. A bare scalar root is the documented boundary (src/fencing/pyjson.ts header) and no fencing artefact has one.

$comment_pysemantics: Inputs for the Python value semantics in src/fencing/pysemantics.ts. renderer.py is idiomatic Python -- x or default, for item in x, needle in haystack, set(x or ()) -- and every one of those idioms is polymorphic where its natural JavaScript translation is narrower. Both mistranslations land on the empty list, and in a fence renderer an empty list means no rules were checked. The values are NAMED rather than embedded because JSON cannot express Python's int/float distinction, and results are compared through repr() so that 'which value came back' is compared rather than 'something truthy came back'.

pysemantics.$comment_values: The shared table. The dump script and the test each hold their own copy keyed by these names; str_0 is the string "0" (truthy in both languages, unlike the int), and list_empty / dict_empty are the two values Python calls FALSY and JavaScript calls truthy -- the inversion that motivates the whole module.
pysemantics.$comment_iterate: `for item in value`. A string yields its CHARACTERS and a mapping its KEYS, which is what makes a malformed hooks group refuse in interlock rather than render; a number and a bool are TypeErrors, and the message is recorded and compared.
pysemantics.$comment_in: Pairs [needle, haystack] for `needle in haystack`, including the SUBSTRING case for a string haystack (permission_modes: "default" makes the bogus mode "faul" a member) and the two TypeErrors.
pysemantics.$comment_set: Element lists for set(). The last two raise: list and dict are unhashable, and renderer.py:335 builds the forbidden-allow exact set that way, so a malformed global config ABORTS the render in interlock instead of refusing it.
pysemantics.$comment_iterate_accepted_deviations: `for item in None` is a TypeError in Python and an empty list here. Deliberate and documented in src/fencing/pysemantics.ts: every call site passes the value through pyOr first, which turns None into the fallback, so the branch is unreachable in the renderer and accepting it keeps the helpers composable in either order. Asserted in BOTH directions, so the day CPython stops raising -- or the day the port starts -- the entry fails loudly instead of licensing nothing.
pysemantics.$comment_set_accepted_deviations: Python's numeric tower makes False == 0 == 0.0, so set() COLLAPSES them into one element and keeps the first; a JavaScript Set compares with SameValueZero and keeps both. Recorded rather than emulated: reproducing Python's numeric equality inside a Set would mean rebuilding hash semantics for a difference that cannot change a fence decision (the forbidden-allow set is only ever probed with strings), and hiding it would leave the port claiming a parity it does not have. Asserted in both directions.
pysemantics.$comment_str: str(), which is repr() for a container and None/True for the scalars.
pysemantics.$comment_mapping_texts: JSON object texts, parsed by each side's loader, for dict.items() and for iteration over a mapping. Texts rather than named values because the property under test IS the key order, and a JavaScript object literal cannot hold it.
